text: Web, email, and file transfer are the services every organization runs, and every one of them follows a conceptual pattern worth knowing cold. HTTP and HTTPS both work the same way: the client sends a request, the server sends back a response. HTTPS is that exact same exchange, just wrapped in TLS encryption so an eavesdropper only sees ciphertext.

A browser sends a GET request for a page, and the server answers with a status code like 200 OK plus the actual content. Nothing about that conversation changes between HTTP and HTTPS — only whether it's locked inside an encrypted tunnel first.

Email is really two separate jobs. SMTP, on port 25, sends mail and relays it between mail servers. Retrieving mail you've already received is a different protocol entirely: POP3 downloads messages to one device and often deletes them from the server, while IMAP keeps the whole mailbox synced across every device, which is why it's the modern default.

FTP moves files but sends everything, including login credentials, in plaintext — insecure on any untrusted network. SFTP does the same job tunneled through SSH encryption, protecting both credentials and file contents. SMB is Windows' native file-sharing protocol, the thing behind every mapped network drive, and also one of the most common paths for lateral movement once an attacker has a foothold.

These three services get attacked constantly because they're exposed to the widest possible audience. Web applications accept input from anyone, which enables injection and cross-site scripting. Email is the leading delivery mechanism for phishing and malware. SMB is how ransomware like WannaCry spread machine to machine across a network in 2017.

Understanding how these protocols actually work — request and response, sending versus retrieving, plaintext versus encrypted — is what lets an analyst tell normal traffic from an attack in progress. Next up: wireless networking and the real security story behind WEP, WPA2, and WPA3.
